target: AI/ML engineering internships (ML infrastructure, LLM applications), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: The bullet opens on a noun stack, 'EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check', and the purpose clause 'to trigger fine-tuning' grammatically attaches to the classifier ('a classifier that rates documents ... to trigger fine-tuning'), not to the check he built. 'its grades' could mean the judge's grades or the classifier's grades. There is no outcome, so it reads as a task.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most ML-infrastructure-relevant bullet on the page, but a reader has to parse it twice to work out that he built a drift monitor that gates retraining. Most skimmers will skip it.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whose grades shift (the judge scoring the classifier's outputs, or the classifier's own score distribution), and what the check replaced (fixed-schedule fine-tuning?)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what the check does in plain words, then the mechanism, and move the scheduler to the end or into Skills. Example shape: 'Built a scheduled LLM-as-judge check that re-grades a production Bedrock document classifier and triggers fine-tuning only when its grades drift past a threshold'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Split a Claude skill into sub-skills backed by Python search and validation tools to stop open-ended model search, which cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s with no quality loss in stress tests
bullet_feedback.problem: Structure rule: 'with no quality loss in stress tests' is an extra clause tacked onto the end after the 'which' result. 'Claude skill', 'sub-skills' and 'LLM workflow generation' are not defined, so a non-engineer cannot say what a workflow is or who generates it.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the headline LLM-applications win. A recruiter keeps '65%' but loses what got faster and for whom.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what a 'workflow' is here (a test-data workflow for developers?) in a few plain words
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the trailing quality clause, or fold it into the main result so the bullet ends on the metric. Replace 'LLM workflow generation' with a short plain noun for what the model produces.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database's permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill's main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: 'which became' grammatically points to 'permission and rate limits', the nearest noun, not to the category tree. 'Redis-cached category tree' is a noun stack. It is also unclear how precomputing keeps lookups within *permission* limits: rate limits make sense, permissions do not.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer will ask 'how does caching solve a permissions problem?' If the answer is not crisp, this claim looks padded.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the permission constraint was (e.g., the skill could not query the table directly at runtime)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder so the result follows its subject directly ('built a cached category tree ... that became the skill's main search tool'), and either explain or drop 'permission'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow tool as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation to make editing smoother, which 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred
bullet_feedback.problem: Five technologies in the middle of the sentence (React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow, Jest) read as a keyword dump. 'to make editing smoother' is vague. 'which ... preferred' attaches to 'editing smoother' and never says preferred over what.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The 90% figure is bolded, so it draws the eye, but without a comparison it is a satisfaction poll, not an outcome. The tech list buries the actual design choice, a visual editor replacing hand-edited configs.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: 'preferred over the legacy tool' (if that was the survey question)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep one or two technologies that explain the design (Electron, the visual flow editor), move the rest to Skills, and state the comparison the 90% refers to.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a topic-scoring research tool and deployed it to dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK to show Amazon Leo's public-policy staff which research topics are popular
bullet_feedback.problem: Ambiguous ownership: 'Co-built' with no indication of which part was his. The middle is a deployment-stack list (Fargate, GitHub Actions, CI/CD, CDK) that does not explain any engineering decision. 'deployed it to dev' is honest but signals the tool never reached users, and the purpose clause comes last, after the tech dump.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A skeptical reader sees keywords plus 'co-' plus 'dev' and discounts the whole bullet. It is the weakest of the three Amazon Leo bullets.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which piece he owned (the scoring logic, or the infra/deploy)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: State his piece first and the purpose second. Keep only the deployment tech that matches the part he owned, or cut this bullet so the stronger two Leo bullets stand out.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built and prompt-tuned a pipeline for a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D to help a vision-language model pick grasps that avoid hitting the table
bullet_feedback.problem: Garden path: 'a robotics project aimed at ICLR that overlays ...' makes the project, not the pipeline, the thing that overlays. 'aimed at ICLR' name-drops a venue with no submission status. There is no result, and 'Built and prompt-tuned' is two verbs for an unclear split of work.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A research reader will ask 'did it get submitted, and did the overlay improve grasp success?' With nothing on the page, the ICLR mention reads as borrowed prestige.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: submission status, or drop the venue; whether any grasp-selection improvement was observed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Put the pipeline's action right after 'pipeline' and move the project context to the end (or into the role line). Cut 'aimed at ICLR' unless a status can be stated.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of Tortuga's Prisma ORM queries to reduce database load and latency for a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: 'Tortuga' is never explained (is it the scheduler's name?). The only number, 20,000+ visits, measures the product's traffic, not the caching work, so 'reduce database load and latency' is an unmeasured intent.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may credit the 20,000 visits to the caching, and an interviewer who asks 'how much did load drop?' exposes the gap.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: that Tortuga is the class scheduler
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the product once, plainly, so the visit count reads as context for scale rather than as a result of the caching. Example shape: 'Added Redis caching in front of the Prisma queries for Tortuga, a class scheduler that drew 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to cut database load'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost
bullet_feedback.problem: 'backtested Java capacity-planning logic' is a noun stack. 'the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching' is a garden path: 'Redshift reserves' reads as a noun pair until the reader backtracks.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the first bullet under the top brand, and it needs a second read to see that Redshift reserves spare EC2 capacity during patching.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the relative pronoun and unstack the adjectives. Example shape: 'Writing Java capacity-planning logic, backtested on past data, that sets bounds on how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift holds in reserve for patching, to balance availability against cost'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building RAG meal suggestions for the official UMD app with SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes, which internal testers rated satisfactory for 93% of meals
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to feed GPT-4o mini real scraped recipes' is an awkward double object that is hard to say aloud. '93% of meals' is ambiguous (meals, or suggested meals?). 'official UMD app' leaves the relationship unclear: is this a contract, and is it live?
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is one of the cleanest RAG examples for an LLM-applications reader, but the clumsy middle hides the design point: grounding the LLM in real recipes.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the feature is shipped or in testing (the 'Building' tense suggests testing)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the grounding clause as a purpose ('so GPT-4o mini suggests only real scraped recipes') and say '93% of suggestions'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: Close to the ideal form. The only gaps are the unclear baseline (34% of per-document or per-batch latency?) and whether 6,000+ is a total or a rate.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is an easy interview follow-up, and it is fine as long as he has the answer ready.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether 6,000+ is total documents or per run/day
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Optional: add 'per run' or 'per day' if accurate. Otherwise leave as is.

page_feedback.problem: The AI/ML Skills line lists 'model fine-tuning' and 'vision-language models', but no bullet shows him fine-tuning a model (the Leo bullet only triggers fine-tuning) or doing more than prompting a VLM. 'Open3D' is a library, not an AI/ML skill.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For an ML-infra screen, 'model fine-tuning' is exactly what an interviewer will probe. If he did not run the fine-tuning himself, this reads as keyword padding.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only skills the bullets back up, or reword to what he did (e.g., 'fine-tuning triggers/evaluation'). Move Open3D to another line.

page_feedback.problem: Skills list technologies that appear in no bullet: OpenSearch, CloudWatch, X-Ray, Docker, uv. The project header also lists 'Linux perf', but the bullet makes no performance claim.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Each unused keyword is a possible interview question with no story behind it. 'Linux perf' next to a bullet with no throughput or latency number invites 'what did perf show?'
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Trim unevidenced items, or make sure he has a one-sentence story ready for each. Consider dropping 'Linux perf' from the project header.

page_feedback.problem: Across the page, three Capital One bullets and two Leo bullets use the 'X to do Y, which Z' frame where 'which' attaches to the nearest noun instead of the intended subject, so the result reads as describing the wrong thing.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This is a repeated comprehension tax. The required sentence form only reads naturally when the 'which' clause sits right after the thing it describes.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: On each bullet, check that the noun just before 'which' is the thing that produced the result, and reorder the clauses where it is not.

page_feedback.problem: The bold on '90%' (a developer-preference survey) gives it the same visual weight as the engineering results 65%, 34% and 50.9M.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Bold should point a skimmer to the strongest wins, and a preference poll is the weakest metric on the page.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices
Header, Education and section ordering: clean single-column layout with consistent right-aligned dates
